opus-5.5.text:
Well, thanks for having me, Peter. So the way I think about it comes from my work in neuroscience. When you look at the brain, one of the things that makes life feel meaningful is actually memory. And memory isn't a recording. We don't remember everything that happens to us; we remember the moments that stood out, the ones that were new, surprising, emotional. If you think back over the last year, you probably don't remember most Tuesdays. You remember the trip, the first time you met someone, the conversation that changed your mind. Those are the anchors, and in a sense your life, as you experience it in retrospect, is just the collection of those anchors.

Now, what technology does, and I say this as someone who loves technology and builds things, is that it's extremely good at removing friction and removing novelty. It optimizes. Your phone learns what you like and gives you more of it. The navigation app takes you the fastest route, so you never get lost and stumble into the weird little café you'd remember for ten years. The feed gives you a steady drip of mild stimulation that feels engaging in the moment but leaves nothing behind. You can scroll for two hours and, at the end, you can't tell me a single thing you saw. From the brain's perspective, those two hours basically didn't happen. They never get encoded as a memory.

So my worry is a quiet one. It isn't that technology is evil. It's that we're trading moments for convenience without noticing the trade. Each individual choice is rational: of course I want the faster route, the better recommendation, the thing I already know I like. But add all of that up and you get days that are smooth, efficient and completely forgettable. And then people reach a certain age, look back, and feel that time flew by and they're not sure what they did with it. That feeling, I think, is very close to what people mean when they say they're missing the meaning of life.

The irony is that the brain actually wants a bit of discomfort. Novelty, uncertainty, and even small mistakes are what make an experience memorable. So the advice I give, and try to follow myself, is to deliberately reintroduce some randomness. Take the wrong turn occasionally. Have the conversation without checking your phone. Do things where you don't know how they'll turn out. That's not anti-technology. It's just recognizing that the thing technology is best at, making life predictable, is exactly the thing that erodes the experiences we end up valuing most.

r001.rationale: The response connects meaning to memorable experiences and warns that technology can make time forgettable, but it does not say that dismissing an activity as pointless because it has little lasting consequence misses what makes life meaningful.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, I should start by saying I'm not a technophobe. I spend most of my life around technology, I use it, I study brains that are shaped by it. So the worry isn't that technology is bad. The worry is more specific than that.

Here's the thing I keep coming back to. The brain is an organ that evolved to solve problems. Hunger, danger, finding a mate, figuring out where you stand in the group. And a lot of what we historically called "meaning" came out of the friction of solving those problems. The effort was the point. You went on a long journey, and the journey changed you, and then when you got the thing, it mattered because of what it cost you.

What technology is very, very good at is removing friction. That's basically the business model of every company in Silicon Valley. Find a place where a human has to struggle a bit, and remove the struggle. And individually, each of those removals looks like a win. I don't have to remember phone numbers. I don't have to get lost. I don't have to be bored in a waiting room, because I have this thing in my pocket that will entertain me for the next forty minutes.

But boredom, for example, is not a bug. Boredom is the brain's way of saying, "nothing in the environment is demanding attention right now, so go inward." That's where you reflect, that's where you consolidate memories, that's where you actually ask yourself, "what do I want? Am I happy? Is this the life I meant to live?" And we've essentially engineered boredom out of existence. The moment the brain gets even slightly quiet, we reach for the phone. So the question never gets asked. Not because people don't care about the answer, but because the window where the question would naturally come up has been filled.

The other piece is that these tools are optimized for a very narrow signal. Engagement. Time on screen. Did you click. And the brain has a hard time distinguishing between "this feels good right now" and "this is good for me." Those are different systems, and the technology is talking almost exclusively to the first one. So you get a life that feels, moment to moment, pretty stimulating, and then you zoom out and there's this strange emptiness, and people can't figure out why. I see this in students, I see it in very successful executives who have everything they thought they wanted.

So when I say people are missing the meaning of life, I don't mean something mystical. I mean something almost mechanical. Meaning requires attention, it requires some struggle, and it requires quiet time for the brain to integrate. And we've built a world that is very efficient at starving all three of those. Not out of malice. Just because that's what sells.

r001.rationale: The response says that effort and struggle can make experiences meaningful, but it does not state that judging an activity pointless because it leaves little lasting consequence misses its meaning.

astra-6.text:
I worry that technology is getting very good at capturing our attention, while we’re not necessarily getting better at deciding where we want our attention to go. Those are two different things. Something can keep you engaged for three hours without being something you would have chosen to spend three hours doing.

And the difficult part is that, in the moment, it can feel perfectly satisfying. There’s always another video, another message, another thing to discover. You don’t get a signal saying, “You’re missing your life.” You just look up and the evening is gone.

I don’t think there’s one meaning of life that everybody has to find. But finding what matters to you takes some space. Sometimes it takes boredom, or a difficult conversation, or staying with a question that doesn’t have an immediate answer. If we fill every one of those moments, we may lose the opportunity to discover what we actually care about.

Technology can help us enormously. My concern is whether we’re using it to live the life we want, or letting whatever captures our attention decide what that life becomes.

r001.rationale: The response discusses attention, personal meaning, and discovering what matters, but it does not say that an activity can be meaningful despite producing little lasting consequence—or that dismissing it as pointless misses its meaning.

sol-6.1.text:
I worry that we’re getting very good at giving people what they want in the moment, without asking whether it’s what they want their life to be about. You open your phone for a minute, and suddenly an hour is gone. Every individual thing you watched might have been entertaining, but you wouldn’t necessarily have chosen to spend that hour that way.

And the things that make life meaningful often don’t compete very well for your attention. Building a relationship, learning something difficult, sitting with a question you can’t answer—these things take time, and sometimes they’re uncomfortable. If you have a device that can take away the discomfort immediately, it becomes very easy to keep reaching for it.

I don’t think technology necessarily takes meaning away. But it can fill all the space in which you might have discovered it. And that’s the concern: you can be entertained all day and still feel that you haven’t really lived the day.

r001.rationale: The response contrasts immediate entertainment with activities it calls meaningful, but it does not say that dismissing an activity as pointless because it has little lasting consequence misses what makes it meaningful.
